title: Miss Sarah Jack of Spanish Town, Jamaica

evidence.paraphrase: A major social/legal change occurs in the storyworld: the emancipation of slaves.
Consequence of unrest: slaves revolt and destroy the estate's buildings.
evidence.quote:
His slaves rose
against him, as they did against other proprietors around him, and burned
down his house and mills, his homestead and offices.

evidence.paraphrase: The abolition of the protective duty on Jamaica sugar is presented as a final economic blow.
evidence.quote:
But even this Mr. Cumming did bear after a while, and kept his shoulder
to the wheel.  He kept his shoulder to the wheel till that third
misfortune came upon him
into the protection duty on Jamaica sugar was
abolished.

evidence.paraphrase: The estate's sugar production steadily declines over time.
evidence.quote:
In the good old times Mr.
Cumming
s sugar produce had spread itself annually over some three
hundred acres; but by degrees this dwindle down to half that extent of
land.

evidence.paraphrase: Narrator contrasts modern readers' view of emancipation with the proprietors' view at the time.
evidence.quote:
It is not perhaps possible that we, now-a-days, should
regard this as a calamity; but it was quite impossible that a Jamaica
proprietor of those days should not have done so.

evidence.paraphrase: Narrator explicitly addresses readers' likely unfamiliarity with West Indian social customs.
evidence.quote:
As a rule they will not
know how thoroughly flirting is an institution in the West
Indies

evidence.paraphrase: Explanation of climatic differences by altitude between Kingston and the mountains.
evidence.quote:
The family of the Leslies lived up near
Newcastle
in the mountains, that is, which stand over Kingston
at a
distance of some eighteen miles from Kingston, but in a climate as
different from that of the town as the climate of Naples is from that of
Berlin.

evidence.paraphrase: Description of altitude and its effect on temperature in the mountains.
evidence.quote:
In the mountains round
Newcastle, some four thousand feet above the sea, it is merely warm
during the day, and cool enough at night to make a blanket desirable.

evidence.paraphrase: Maurice reacts with jealousy and resolves to give up on Marian.
evidence.quote:
I will have nothing more to say to
her,
said Maurice to himself, scowling.

evidence.paraphrase: Marian breaks down in tears, confessing her love for Maurice.
evidence.quote:
Oh, Fanny, I do love him, I do love him so dearly! and now
he will never come to me again!
